name: Nikhil Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a picking team on nights at a big chilled-food distribution centre, the one that feeds about ninety supermarkets. I start at ten, we pick yoghurt, cheese, ready meals and fresh meat onto roll cages until the trucks leave at six. I wear a headset that tells me the aisle and the quantity, and I say a check number back. I'm proud that my team hits the rate without anyone getting hurt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. There's eleven of us and I know whose back is bad and who's got a kid teething. What wears me out is the cold, it's three degrees in there all night, and the rate going up every spring without anyone asking us. My partner Sasha works days at a care home, so we mostly see each other on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the break room: told you so. Every year management shows us a slide about the future and every year we're still pushing cages. I'd post something in the union group chat like, the robots are late again, lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays roughly where it is, which isn't bad but isn't easy. I keep my lead job, the pay creeps up a bit, and the rent goes up faster. The cold and the nights are still the real problem, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep pushing the union on the night allowance, because that's where the money is. I'd put the same hundred and fifty a month into savings that I do now. Maybe I'd finally sort the warehouse forklift licence renewal before it lapses in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of tiredness. It's the devil you know. I'd sleep fine, apart from the fact that I sleep in the day anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rate goes up every spring. In this world, what happens to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rate still goes up, because that's what the company does whether there's AI or not. Last spring they put it from 160 cases an hour to 172, and two of my older pickers struggled. In this picture I'm still fighting that every year, so it's not like everything is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you still be keeping an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doreen, who's fifty-eight and has been there twenty years, and Kofi, who's new and doesn't speak up. If the company saves a bit with software, it won't go to them. I'd still be the one making sure they get their breaks.

say: The **robots are late again**, and the bosses' future slides never match the shop floor.
Night pickers still need a **fair night allowance**, with or without AI.
think: My **lead job** stays, but rent keeps rising faster than my **pay**.
The cold, the nights and the **yearly rate rise** are the real pressures on my body.
do: **Keep working** the night shift and push the union on the **night allowance**.
Put **£150 a month** into savings, the same as now.
Renew the **forklift licence** before it lapses in March.
feel: Mostly **relief**, with the ordinary **tiredness** of nights.
S0.quote: Last spring they put it from 160 cases an hour to 172, and two of my older pickers struggled.
fieldNote: He judges the future by the **pick rate**, which already rises every spring without AI.
His loyalty is to his **crew**; he names the older and newest pickers unprompted.
Even with nothing radical changing, the **cold and nights** keep him from feeling calm.

steps.text: Keep leading the night picking team at the chilled-food centre
Push the union rep for a higher night allowance
Keep putting £150 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the office's problem first, not ours, and I'd mean it. Online I'd be sharing union stuff about making sure the savings get shared, not just handed to shareholders. I'd say the company owes us a seat at the table before they buy anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I know the hands-on part buys me time but not forever. The planners and the transport office will shrink first, and then the money they save goes into the next thing, which is machines on our floor. I'm not good with new tech, so if the job changes shape I'm worried I'll be behind the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get us to ask for a written agreement on retraining before any robots come in. I'd start putting two hundred a month aside instead of one fifty and cancel the gym I never go to. I'd not touch any AI app myself, I'd rather keep my head down and be the best picker on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. It's like when they announce a meeting and don't say what it's about. You spend the whole shift guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office goes first. Has anything like that already happened where you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The shift planner job went to software last year at our sister site, and the planner ended up on the loading bay after fifteen years. Ruth had done that planning since before I started. People said she was lucky to keep a job at all, which made me angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sasha about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine for now but I'm putting more away. Sasha would say I should learn the new systems, and she'd be right, and I'd probably still drag my feet. That's me, I know it.

say: This hits the **office first**, and any savings must be **shared**.
The company owes pickers **a seat** at the table before buying **machines**.
think: Hands-on work buys **time, not safety**; office savings will fund floor machines next.
I'm slow with tech, so I fear falling **behind younger pickers**.
do: **Attend** every union meeting and press for a written **retraining agreement**.
Raise savings to **£200 a month** and cancel the unused gym membership.
feel: A **knot in the stomach**, like waiting for an unexplained meeting.
S1.quote: The shift planner job went to software last year at our sister site, and the planner ended up on the loading bay after fifteen years.
fieldNote: A real case, a planner moved to the **loading bay**, makes the risk concrete for him.
He admits he'll **drag his feet** on new systems even when his partner is right.
His answer to change is **collective**: agreements first, his own learning last.

steps.text: Press the union for a written retraining deal before robots arrive
Cancel the gym membership he never uses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that steps in, and I'd say it loudly. Online I'd be signing every petition going for a robot tax or a shorter working week. At work I'd tell the crew to stick together and not let them pick us off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in that building by 2031. Picking is the most robot-shaped job there is, because it's literally a list of things to fetch. I've got a few months of savings, Sasha's job is probably safer than mine, and I don't know what else I'm good at besides this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd still go to work but I'd be the loudest voice in the union for a redundancy deal and retraining money. I'd look at the care home where Sasha works, because people will still want a human holding their hand. I'd stop the car finance plan we'd been talking about and just keep the old Corsa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, and angry underneath it. I'd be lying awake at two in the afternoon thinking about it, which is my two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What do you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them to get something in place, because I'm not quick to change and I know it. Probably a care course at the college, nights off on Wednesdays. The thinking AI first means the planners and transport office go in 2028, and that tells me exactly what's coming for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out goes first, then the holiday to see Sasha's family in the summer. The rent is the thing I can't cut. We'd last maybe four months on her wage plus my savings if I got let go.

say: We need **unions** and a government that steps in, like a **robot tax**.
The crew must **stick together** so management can't pick us off one by one.
think: Picking is the most **robot-shaped job**; I expect to be gone by **2031**.
With **a few months saved**, I don't know what else I'm good at.
do: **Push hard** in the union for a **redundancy deal** and retraining money.
Start a **care course** at the college on Wednesday nights.
**Drop the car finance** plan and keep driving the old Corsa.
feel: Losing sleep in the **daytime hours** he normally sleeps.
S2.quote: Picking is the most robot-shaped job there is, because it's literally a list of things to fetch.
fieldNote: He reads the **2028 office cuts** as a direct warning about the 2031 robots.
Though resistant to change, the **three-year gap** pushes him toward a care course.
His partner's **care home job** feels safer than his and becomes his escape route.

steps.text: Lead the union push for a redundancy and retraining deal
Enrol on a Wednesday night care course at the local college
Drop the car finance plan and keep the old Corsa running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd have more time to organise it properly. I'd say at work that we've got five years to get a deal in writing, so let's not waste them. I'd be pushing for a national campaign, not just our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm thirty-two when the thinking stuff lands and about thirty-five when the robots do. That's young enough to start over, which helps. But I'd still be starting over from the bottom of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on as lead and save harder, maybe two fifty a month, for two or three years. I'd do the care course properly, one evening a week, and maybe pick up a few bank shifts at Sasha's care home to see if I can stand it. I'd keep pushing the union to get retraining money signed before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like a long worry than a sharp one. I'd have time to get used to the idea, which is how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Does that change what you'd do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes it a lot. With two years I'd be panicking into something, but with five years I can try care shifts and quit them if I hate them. I'd find out before I need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow to change. With five years, is that still a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still a problem, because I'll put things off. Sasha would have to keep on at me. If I'm honest, I'd probably wait until the first robots turn up at the sister site before I actually signed up for anything.

say: We've got **five years** to get a deal **in writing**, so don't waste them.
This needs a **national campaign**, not just one warehouse.
think: At **thirty-five** I'd be young enough to start over, but **from the bottom**.
Five years makes a career change **possible**, though not comfortable.
do: Save **£250 a month** for two or three years while staying team lead.
Try **bank shifts** at the care home to test the work.
Keep pushing the union to sign **retraining money** before 2031.
feel: A **long, slow worry** instead of a sharp one.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be panicking into something, but with five years I can try care shifts and quit them if I hate them.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **test care work** before he needs it.
He predicts his own **procrastination**, saying he'd wait for robots at the sister site.
He still expects to **lose the picking job**, so the mood stays high even with time.

steps.text: Save £250 a month for the next two or three years
Finish the evening care course at the college
Work some bank shifts at the care home to try it out
Push the union for retraining money signed before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do this right, so there's no excuse. I'd be telling people to vote for whoever backs retraining and a shorter week. At work I'd say keep calm but keep the union strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-nine when the robots come for the picking. That's mid-career, and I'd have had time to drift into something else. Part of me knows I'd use the time to put it off, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, honestly, not much: keep my lead job, keep the savings going at two hundred. I'd vote and go to union meetings like I already do. Maybe in year three or four I'd start the care course, once I'd seen what happens to the office lot in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but it doesn't go away. Ten years of warning feels like a bill that's due in ten years, because you still know the bill is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you be doing in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd just carry on, really. Lead the crew, do my nights, keep an eye on Doreen's back. I don't move until I have to, that's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new picker starting under you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new picker that this job will pay the rent for a few years but not for life. Get a second skill while you're young, and join the union on your first day.

say: With **ten years**, governments have **no excuse** not to plan properly.
People should **vote** for parties backing **retraining** and a shorter week.
think: At **thirty-nine** the robots arrive, which is **mid-career** for me.
I know I'd use the extra time to **put things off**.
do: **Keep leading** the night crew and saving **£200** a month.
Start the **care course** around year three or four, after watching the office cuts.
feel: **Calmer**, but like a **bill due** in ten years that never leaves his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning feels like a bill that's due in ten years, because you still know the bill is there.
fieldNote: The decade lets his **resistance** win in the short term: he plans to wait.
His advice to a new picker, **get a second skill**, is advice he isn't taking.
He still expects the **picking job to go**, so his worry is quieter but real.

steps.text: Keep leading the night picking crew for the first few years
Vote for parties backing retraining and a shorter working week
Wait to watch the 2036 office cuts before starting the care course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, no question. Two years for the office and five for us isn't enough for someone like me who's slow to switch. What would help is a proper deal: redundancy pay, paid retraining at a college, and the union in the room when the machines get bought.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. Nobody wants to do this job at fifty, my knees already click in the freezer. Picking is a young person's job that pays the rent, and the robots will be taking a job that hurts people. I just want the people to land somewhere.

headlineQuote: Picking is a young person's job that pays the rent, and the robots will be taking a job that hurts people.
portrait: Nikhil, 27, leads an eleven-person **night picking crew** in a chilled-food distribution centre.
He is a committed **union man** who measures change by the yearly pick rate rise.
He avoids new tech and admits he'll **drag his feet**, even when partner Sasha pushes.
In the fast AGI picture he expects to be **out by 2031** and eyes care work.
With ten years he would **mostly wait**, though he knows picking won't last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two to five years is too short for someone **slow** to switch.
whatWouldHelp: A **redundancy deal**, paid **college retraining** and the union present when machines are bought.
